evidence: createRouter() builds an Express Router and registers routes with router.get/router.post. This is transport/framework wiring, which fits infrastructure.
Routes such as router.post('/staff/orders/:id/ship', staffOnly, orders.changeStatus('ship')) only pass an action name to the controller. The file does no state-transition logic itself.
staffOnly is a RequestHandler injected from outside. The file only attaches it to routes and does not decide how authorization works.
The Controllers interface is a plain grouping of HTTP controllers with no behaviour.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The file passes. src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts only wires HTTP transport. It builds an Express Router, maps HTTP verbs and paths to controller handlers, and adds the injected staffOnly middleware to the /staff routes. All of that is framework and transport work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer. The file has no domain logic: no validation, no checks on order state transitions, no pricing or stock rules, and no persistence. The calls to orders.changeStatus('pay'|'cancel'|...) only pass an action name, and the actual work is left to the controllers. Choosing which routes need the staff key is a route-level access-control decision made with injected middleware. That is a normal transport concern, not a business rule built into this file.
